summary: Tunisia lets citizens of a broad list of countries — the EU, UK, US, Canada, Japan, most of Europe and many Arab, African and Asian states — enter visa-free for up to 90 days. Nationalities outside the list apply for a consular visa; Israeli passport holders are not admitted.

passportValidity.text: Tunisia officially requires a passport valid for the duration of your stay, but airlines and border officers commonly expect 3–6 months' validity — carry more than the minimum.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tunisia

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required for travelers over 1 year of age arriving from countries with risk of yellow fever transmission.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tunisia

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not checked for visa-exempt tourists, but medical coverage is strongly recommended; visa applicants may be asked for proof of insurance.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tunisia

onwardTicket.text: Border officers and airlines regularly ask visa-exempt visitors for a return or onward ticket and accommodation details — package tourists are rarely questioned, independent travelers should have both to hand.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tunisia

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; officers may ask visitors to show sufficient means for their stay.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tunisia

currencyLimits.text: The Tunisian dinar is non-convertible — bringing dinars in or out of the country is prohibited. Declare foreign cash above the published threshold (roughly TND 20,000 equivalent) on arrival, and declare any amount you may want to take out again: re-exporting undeclared foreign currency is capped. Keep all exchange receipts to reconvert leftover dinars at departure.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tunisia

notes: Change money only at banks, exchange offices and hotels, and keep the receipts — you will need them to change dinars back before you leave.
Drones may not be brought into Tunisia without prior authorization and are routinely held by customs.

payments.text: Cards are accepted at hotels, larger restaurants and supermarkets in cities and resort areas, but souks, taxis, and small towns run on cash. ATMs are widespread in urban and tourist areas.

safety.text: The main tourist areas — Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse, Djerba — are generally safe with normal precautions. Governments advise against travel to the Libyan and Algerian border zones and the Chaambi mountain area, and a state of emergency remains formally in place.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Tunisia Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: April to June and September to October offer warm seas and pleasant heat without the peak-summer crowds; mid-summer is very hot inland and in the south.

idp.text: Tunisia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Tunisia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Tunisia yet.

tips.text: The dinar is a closed currency — you cannot buy it before you arrive or take it home. Exchange money in Tunisia, keep every receipt, and reconvert leftover dinars at the airport before departure (reconversion without receipts is refused).

Stays beyond your allowance incur a per-week fine collected when you leave. If you need longer than 90 days, apply for an extension through the local police (Sûreté Nationale) well before your time runs out.

Avoid the immediate border areas with Libya and Algeria and the Chaambi mountain region — governments warn of terrorism and military operations there. The Sahara south of Remada is a designated military zone requiring authorization.
Independent travelers should carry proof of accommodation and a return or onward ticket — border officers ask for these far more often than they do with package tourists.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Tunisia?
faq.answer: Most Western tourists do not. Citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Japan, and much of Europe, the Arab world, Africa and Latin America can stay visa-free for up to 90 days. Nationalities outside the exemption list — including most of South Asia and many African states — need a consular visa before travel.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Tunisia without a visa?
faq.answer: 90 days for most exempt nationalities (South Koreans get 30 days). Longer stays require an extension through the local police; overstays are fined per week when you exit.

faq.question: Can I bring Tunisian dinars in or out of the country?
faq.answer: No — the dinar is non-convertible and its import and export are prohibited. Exchange foreign currency inside Tunisia, keep the receipts, and reconvert leftover dinars before departure. Large amounts of foreign cash must be declared on arrival.

faq.question: Can Israeli citizens visit Tunisia?
faq.answer: No — Israeli passport holders are not admitted to Tunisia.

faq.question: Is Tunisia safe for tourists?
faq.answer: The coastal resorts and main cities are generally safe with normal precautions, and tourism infrastructure is well developed. Avoid the Libyan and Algerian border zones and the Chaambi mountains, which carry government travel warnings.

faq.question: Do I need a return ticket to enter Tunisia?
faq.answer: Formally entry is at the officer's discretion, but airlines and border police regularly ask visa-exempt visitors for a return or onward ticket and accommodation details — carry both.
